titleText.es: Tras esto, la paleta de pong fue a destruir el cuartel general de Atari pero, por error, se metió en el juego The Matrix Reloaded. Joder, qué difícil fue explicárselo.
titleText.en: After this, the Pong paddle went to destroy Atari headquarters, but by mistake it ended up inside the game The Matrix Reloaded. Damn, that was hard to explain to him.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish translation uses Joder, a stronger exclamation than the original xkcd title text's “Boy.”

regions.labelEs: ¿QUÉ HARÍAMOS SI LOS OPONENTES DE IA DE LOS VIDEOJUEGOS SE VOLVIESEN TAN INTELIGENTES COMO PARA CUESTIONARSE LA "MATRIX" EN LA QUE ESTÁN?

applications.explanationEn: Qué carries a written accent because it directly asks what. The unaccented connector que has a different job.
Haríamos is the conditional, or “would,” form of hacer for we. It supplies the imagined result.
Si introduces the imagined condition. It has no accent when it means “if.”
Volviesen is the plural -se form used for the imagined condition; the equally valid -ra form would be volvieran.
Se and volviesen form volverse for a plural subject, while inteligentes names the new quality. Tan only adds the degree of that quality.
Tan gives the degree, como para introduces what that degree makes possible, and cuestionarse remains in its dictionary form.
En supplies “in,” la matches the feminine name Matrix, and que links back to that name. Together they introduce its location.
Están is a plural form of estar because it locates the people or things being discussed.
The attached se points the questioning back toward the plural opponents rather than toward a separate listener.

regions.labelEs: ¡UN MOMENTO! ¡NADA DE ESTO ES REAL! ¡PUEDO VER A TRAVÉS DEL MUNDO! ¡PUEDO VER EL CÓDIGO! ¡SOY EL ELEGIDO!

applications.explanationEn: The fixed exclamation signals a sudden interruption or realization rather than merely counting one unit of time.
Nada comes before de esto, so it means none or nothing out of the situation being considered.
Es is a form of ser used for a claim about what the surrounding situation is.
A través de forms the reusable expression, and de combines with the masculine article el to make del.
Soy is the first-person form of ser because the speaker is declaring an identity.
The article el turns the describing word elegido into a name for the chosen person: “the chosen one.”

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

cards.answerEn: we would do; we would make
cards.noteEn: Haríamos is the conditional form of hacer for nosotros, or “we.” The conditional often describes what would happen in an imagined situation.

cards.questionEn: How do you describe an imagined “if…, …would…” situation?
cards.answerEn: Use si followed by a hypothetical past verb form for the condition, and use a “would” form for the result.
cards.noteEn: Spanish calls the condition's verb form the imperfect subjunctive. It often ends in -ra or -se, as in tuviera or tuviese. The result uses the conditional, often ending in -ría, as in haría. In this pattern, do not put the conditional directly after si.

example.en: If I had time, I would travel more.

cards.noteEn: IA is the Spanish abbreviation for inteligencia artificial. The initials appear in the opposite order from English because inteligencia comes before artificial.

cards.answerEn: marks a change affecting them (part of volverse, “to become”)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something becomes a certain way?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of volverse followed by a describing word for the new state.
cards.noteEn: The short part of volverse changes to me, te, se, nos, os, or se to match who changes, and volver changes for the person and time. The describing word—called an adjective—can also change for gender or number. Volver without the short pronoun usually means “to return.”

example.es: Con el tiempo, se volvieron pacientes.

cards.answerEn: they became; they were to become (in an imagined situation)
cards.noteEn: Volviesen is a plural hypothetical past form of volverse, “to become.” The equivalent -ra form, volvieran, has the same meaning here.

example.es: Si se volviesen famosos, viajarían más.
example.en: If they became famous, they would travel more.

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish say that someone is kind enough to help, or so kind that they help?
cards.answerEn: Put tan before the describing word, then como para, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form—called the infinitive—is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. This pattern says that a quality reaches the degree needed for the following action. It is different from the ordinary comparison tan… como, which means “as… as.”

example.es: Fue tan generosa como para ayudarnos.
example.en: She was generous enough to help us.

cards.answerEn: to; enough to (as part of como para)
to question; to ask oneself about
cards.noteEn: The ending -se points the questioning back toward the person doing it. Cuestionarse algo means to question something for oneself rather than simply asking another person a question.

example.en: She began to question her decisions.

cards.answerEn: references The Matrix, where Neo discovers a simulated world and becomes “the One”
cards.noteEn: In The Matrix, computer code underlies the world people perceive. Neo learns to see that code and bend the simulation's physical rules. Other stories can invoke the film by treating an apparently solid world as a simulation whose rules can be discovered or broken.

cards.questionEn: How do you say forms such as “in which,” “with whom,” or “for whom” when referring back to a person or thing?
cards.answerEn: Put the needed preposition before el que, la que, los que, or las que, matching the earlier person or thing.
cards.noteEn: A preposition is a short relationship word such as en (“in”), con (“with”), or para (“for”). Choose el, la, los, or las to match the gender and number of the person or thing being described; que itself does not change. English may use “which” for a thing or “who” or “whom” for a person.

example.es: Esta es la silla en la que me siento.
example.en: This is the chair that I sit in.

cards.answerEn: the feminine article in la que; helps mean which, who, or whom

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.answerEn: they are (in a place or state)

cards.promptEs: ser para identidad · estar para ubicación
cards.questionEn: Which Spanish “to be” verb says what something is, and which says where it is?
cards.answerEn: Use ser for identity or a defining description; use estar for the location of a person or thing.
cards.noteEn: This contrast is not simply permanent versus temporary. Forms of ser such as soy and es identify or describe what something is. Forms of estar such as están normally locate people and things. Events are a common exception: Spanish uses ser to say where or when an event takes place.

example.es: El museo es famoso y está en Madrid.
example.en: The museum is famous and is in Madrid.

cards.questionEn: What does ¡Un momento! mean when someone interrupts or suddenly realizes something?
cards.answerEn: It means “Wait a moment!” or “Hold on!”
cards.noteEn: This fixed conversational interruption can ask someone to pause, or it can announce that the speaker has just noticed something important. Its function is broader than literally measuring one moment.

example.es: ¡Un momento! Creo que tengo la llave.
example.en: Hold on! I think I have the key.

cards.noteEn: Before de plus a thing or situation, nada can mean “none” or “nothing” out of that set. This use does not need a separate no before it when nada itself comes before the verb.
Esto is a neutral demonstrative for an unidentified thing, fact, or whole situation. It is not used directly before a noun.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; part of a través de (“through”)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something goes or can be seen through something?
cards.answerEn: Use a través de before the thing: it means “through” or “across.”
cards.noteEn: Keep all three parts together. Before masculine singular el, de and el combine as del: a través del bosque. Before a feminine noun, use a través de la, as in a través de la ventana. The expression can describe literal passage or a figurative means.

example.es: La luz entra a través de la ventana.
example.en: The light comes in through the window.

cards.answerEn: part of a través de, “through” or “across”

cards.noteEn: Del is the required contraction of de + el. It can mean “of the” or “from the,” depending on context.
Elegido is the describing form made from elegir, “to choose.” With an article, el elegido or la elegida can name the person who was chosen.
